answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering node in a per-layer TE network. It is the node-level forwarding/switching abstraction exposed by the TE topology, rather than necessarily a one-to-one physical device.
answers.example: ROADM R1 represented as a node in the OTN-layer TE topology.
answers.relations: It is part of i.tetopo; i.tp, i.ttp, i.cmatrix, and i.tcep may be associated with or located on it; i.telink connects it to other TE nodes.

answers.gloss: A node-owned termination point at which a TE link terminates.
answers.example: The termination point on R1 facing R2 for the R1–R2 TE link.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and terminates i.telink. It can participate in a client/server supporting relationship represented by i.stp.

answers.gloss: The supporting relationship by which a client-layer termination point is supported by a server-layer termination point. It denotes the adaptation/support association, not merely an independently standing termination point.
answers.example: An OTN termination point at R1 supported by an optical-layer termination point at the same location.
answers.relations: It relates termination points across client and server layers and has a supports relation to i.tp; it captures adaptation between the corresponding layer contexts.

answers.gloss: The point at which a TE tunnel originates or terminates—a tunnel trail head. It is not, by definition, an external customer-facing service-access point, although an implementation could associate one with such access.
answers.example: The A1 trail head of the A1–A3 ODU2 tunnel.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and originates or terminates i.tunnel. It is semantically distinct from the link-facing i.tp and the intra-node tunnel endpoint i.tcep.

answers.gloss: An end-to-end traffic-engineered tunnel that realizes connectivity for a service. It is the TE construct realizing the service, not necessarily the externally offered service contract itself.
answers.example: The A1–A3 ODU2 TE tunnel routed through the OTN network.
answers.relations: It begins and ends at i.ttp, traverses resources represented by i.tetopo, contains or is associated with i.tcep endpoints, and may be identified with an i.otnlabel multiplex allocation.

answers.gloss: An OTN switching/TE label that expresses the tributary-slot and tributary-port-number multiplexing allocation used for an OTN connection. It records the allocated multiplex position; through that allocation it reflects structure such as an ODU2 carried in an OTU4, but it is not a general-purpose description of every layer-protocol characteristic.
answers.example: The TS/TPN values selecting the tributary slots occupied by an ODU2 within an OTU4.
answers.relations: It labels i.tunnel and identifies the OTN multiplex resources allocated to that tunnel.

answers.gloss: A node's connectivity matrix describing or constraining which internal connections are permitted between its termination points.
answers.example: R2's matrix allowing cross-connection from its R1-facing termination point to its R3-facing termination point while disallowing unsupported combinations.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and governs permissible internal connectivity among termination points of that node.

answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering link connecting TE nodes within a layer network.
answers.example: The OTN-layer R1–R2 TE link.
answers.relations: It is between i.tenode instances, is terminated at its ends by i.tp instances, and is contained in i.tetopo.

answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering network/topology for a particular layer.
answers.example: The OTN-layer TE network containing R1, R2, R3, and their OTN TE links.
answers.relations: It contains i.tenode and i.telink, and provides the topology over which i.tunnel is engineered. This model treats it as layer-specific rather than as one intrinsically multilayer topology, although multiple layer topologies can be related externally.

answers.gloss: An endpoint of a tunnel connection within a node.
answers.example: The connection endpoint belonging to the A1–A3 tunnel on R1.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and part of i.tunnel. Unlike i.ttp, it describes a connection endpoint in the node/tunnel realization rather than specifically the end-to-end trail head.

answers.gloss: A forwarding node in the single multi-layer topology. It is a topology-level forwarding/switching abstraction and may represent a device such as a ROADM, without asserting that every node must be a one-to-one physical device.
answers.example: ROADM R1 in the OTN-over-optical topology.
answers.relations: It is part of t.topo. Node-owned constructs include t.ltp, t.sip, t.nrg, and t.cep; t.link connects nodes, and t.translink expresses adaptation at a node.

answers.gloss: A node-owned edge point at which a topological link terminates.
answers.example: The R1 edge point facing R2.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and terminates t.link. This model does not assert an aggregation relation between t.ltp and layer-specific t.cep objects, so such aggregation should not be inferred from the concept definition.

answers.gloss: A link-like representation of adaptation between layer contexts at a node, rather than an ordinary inter-node forwarding link.
answers.example: The OTU4-to-ODU2 adaptation at R1.
answers.relations: It is at t.node and adapts the layer/multiplex structure represented by t.lpq. It is distinct from t.link, which connects nodes. Semantically it expresses a client/server adaptation association, though this model packages that association as a transitional link rather than directly as a termination-point support edge.

answers.gloss: A point through which an external client service accesses the network.
answers.example: The customer-facing ODU2 hand-off at A1.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and accesses t.cs. It is an externally exposed service-access abstraction, distinct from t.cep, which is an endpoint in the internal realization of a connection; it is not defined merely as a tunnel trail head.

answers.gloss: An offered or requested end-to-end connectivity service across the network, not the routed connection or tunnel construct that realizes it.
answers.example: The A1-to-A3 ODU2 connectivity service.
answers.relations: It uses t.sip access points, is realized by connection endpoints represented by t.cep, is qualified by t.lpq, and operates over t.topo.

answers.gloss: A qualifier describing the layer-protocol and multiplexing structure of a signal.
answers.example: ODU2 mapped into an OTU4 server signal.
answers.relations: It qualifies t.cs and is involved in the adaptation expressed by t.translink. It describes multiplex/layer structure; it does not identify a concrete allocated tributary-slot or tributary-port-number switching label.

answers.gloss: A group of rules constraining which ports or termination constructs may be cross-connected within a node.
answers.example: The permitted cross-connect combinations at R2.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and governs intra-node switching possibilities. It is semantically matrix-like, but is represented as a rule group and need not be an exhaustive tabular enumeration of every possible endpoint pair.

answers.gloss: A topological link between two forwarding nodes.
answers.example: The R1-to-R2 link.
answers.relations: It is between t.node instances, terminated by t.ltp instances, and contained in t.topo. Because t.topo is the model's single multi-layer topology, t.link is not defined solely by membership in a separate per-layer topology, although a link can still carry layer context.

answers.gloss: The single multi-layer topology describing the managed domain.
answers.example: The OTN-over-optical domain topology.
answers.relations: It contains t.node and t.link and is the topology over which t.cs is provided. Unlike a strictly per-layer topology model, it intrinsically accommodates multiple related layers in one topology.

answers.gloss: An endpoint of a connection within a node.
answers.example: The endpoint on R1 belonging to the A1-to-A3 service realization.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and part of the realization of t.cs. It is an internal connection endpoint rather than an external service-access point. The supplied model asserts no direct t.cep-to-t.ltp relation.

proposals.rationale: Both denote a topology-level forwarding/switching node and can represent ROADM R1. The main modeling difference is that t.node resides in one multi-layer topology while i.tenode is exposed in a per-layer TE topology.
Both are node-owned edge termination points at which an inter-node topological or TE link terminates.

Both express client/server adaptation or support between layer contexts. They differ representationally: t.translink packages adaptation as a transitional link related to layer qualification, while i.stp directly relates client- and server-layer termination points.

Both describe or constrain permissible intra-node cross-connections among ports or termination constructs. A node rule group may be rule-based rather than a complete matrix, but the governed switching semantics coincide.
Both are topology links between forwarding nodes, terminated by node-owned termination points. Their primary difference follows from multi-layer versus per-layer topology organization.

Both are topology containers for forwarding nodes and links and provide the topological context for engineered connectivity. The correspondence is qualified because t.topo is intrinsically a single multi-layer domain topology, whereas i.tetopo is defined for a particular layer.
Both denote an endpoint of a realized connection or tunnel within a node, as distinct from an external service-access point or a trail head specifically marking the end of the end-to-end tunnel.

ratifications.reason: Both denote a topology-level forwarding/switching node abstraction that may represent a device such as ROADM R1. Placement in a multilayer versus per-layer topology is a modeling-context difference, not a change to the node concept itself.
Both are node-owned edge points at which an inter-node topological or TE link terminates.

Both express the client/server adaptation or support association between layer contexts. TAPI packages it as a link-like transitional construct, while the TEAS model represents the supporting relationship between termination points.
Both constrain permissible internal cross-connections among a node's termination constructs. Rule-group versus matrix representation does not alter the governed switching semantics.
Both denote an inter-node topological traffic-engineering link terminated by node-owned termination points. Their topology-layer organization differs, but the link abstraction corresponds.

They are closely related topology containers but do not denote the same scoped object: t.topo is intrinsically the single multilayer domain topology, whereas i.tetopo is one particular layer's TE network. Several i.tetopo instances could correspond to layer views within one t.topo, so exact concept correspondence is not justified.
Both denote an internal node endpoint belonging to a realized end-to-end connection or tunnel, distinct from an external service-access point.
